summary: Defines the AES-XCBC-MAC-96 message authentication algorithm and how it is used with IPsec. It builds on the CBC-MAC idea, which is secure only for messages of one fixed length, and extends it to handle messages of any length. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3566 defines a way to check that an IPsec packet has not been altered and came from who it claims to. It builds the check out of AES, the encryption algorithm, run in a mode that normally only works on messages of one fixed length. The memo adds a small extension that makes it work on messages of any length, and shortens the result to 96 bits, the size the IPsec Authentication Header expects.

questions: why is cbc-mac not secure for variable length messages
how does xcbc-mac use three keys
how long is the aes-xcbc-mac-96 authenticator
subtitle: A message authentication code built from AES that stays secure for messages of any length, for use with IPsec ESP and AH.

tldr.problem: A message authentication code has to work on messages of any length, because IP datagrams vary in size. The classic CBC-MAC construction only stays secure for a message of one pre-selected length, and for a second message it is trivial to produce a forgery from the code of a first one.
tldr.mechanism: The memo takes AES in CBC mode and adds the XCBC-MAC extensions. Three keys are derived from the 128-bit secret key, and the way the final, possibly short, block is padded and mixed distinguishes a message that is a whole number of blocks long from one that is not, so two different messages of different lengths cannot produce the same code.
tldr.outcome: The result is secure for messages of arbitrary length, and the code is truncated to 96 bits, which is the default length for the IPsec Authentication Header. The memo also fixes the key length at 128 bits, says the three derived keys must not be used anywhere else, and supplies seven test vectors that implementations can check themselves against.

facts.value: 384 bits: 128 for the AES key plus twice the block size

facts.label: Authenticator length
facts.value: 96 bits, the leftmost bits of the 128-bit value

today: RFC 3566 is an Internet standards track document at the Proposed Standard level, and it has not been obsoleted. It defines the AES-XCBC-MAC-96 authenticator, which IANA has registered as AH transform identifier 9 and AH/ESP authentication algorithm value 9.

sections.title: Why a New Authentication Algorithm
sections.content:
Message authentication provides data integrity and data origin authentication with respect to the original message source. A message authentication code, or MAC, is a key-dependent one way hash function. One popular way to construct a MAC algorithm is to use a block cipher together with the Cipher-Block-Chaining mode of operation.

The classic CBC-MAC algorithm is secure for messages of a pre-selected fixed length, but it has been shown to be insecure across messages of varying lengths, such as the kind found in typical IP datagrams. In fact it is trivial to produce forgeries for a second message given the MAC of a prior one.

This memo specifies the use of AES in CBC mode with a set of extensions to overcome that limitation, and the resulting algorithm is named AES-XCBC-MAC-96. Using the AES block cipher, with its increased block size of 128 bits and increased key length of 128 bits, gives the new algorithm the ability to withstand continuing advances in crypto-analytic techniques and computational capability.

AES-XCBC-MAC-96 is used as an authentication mechanism within the IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload and Authentication Header protocols. The goal of the algorithm is to ensure that the datagram is authentic and cannot be modified in transit. The data integrity and data origin authentication it provides depend on the scope of the distribution of the secret key: if the key is known only to the source and the destination, the algorithm provides both data origin authentication and data integrity for datagrams sent between the two parties. Only a party holding the identical key can verify the hash.

IANA has assigned AH Transform Identifier 9 to AH_AES-XCBC-MAC and AH/ESP Authentication Algorithm Value 9 to AES-XCBC-MAC.
sections.plainLanguage: IPsec needs a check on every packet, and packets differ in size. The old way of building that check out of a block cipher only worked for one fixed size, so this memo gives a fixed-up version that works for any size, using AES.

sections.title: Basic CBC-MAC and Its Limitation
sections.content:
CBC-MAC uses a block cipher for encryption, where the block cipher transforms b bits of plaintext to b bits of ciphertext. The basic CBC-MAC with obligatory 10* padding over a b-bit block cipher is calculated as follows for a message M.

First, a single 1 bit is appended to M, then the minimum number of 0 bits is appended so that the length of M is a multiple of b. The padded message is broken into n blocks M[1] to M[n], each of b bits. E[0] is defined as 0x00000000000000000000000000000000. Then, for each block M[i], the block is XORed with E[i-1] and the result is encrypted with the key K, yielding E[i]. Finally E[n] is the b-bit authenticator.

Basic CBC-MAC with obligatory 10* padding has been shown to be secure for messages up to, but not including, a pre-selected fixed length, which is a multiple of the block size. It is not suitable for IPsec for two reasons. Any IPsec authenticator must be able to handle messages of arbitrary length, and the basic CBC-MAC cannot securely handle messages that exceed the pre-selected fixed length. And for messages shorter than the pre-selected fixed length, padding the message up to that length may necessitate additional encryption operations, adding an unacceptable computational penalty.

The fix in this memo is not to the padding alone but to the treatment of the last block, which is what tells a receiver whether the message was an exact number of blocks long or whether a final short block was padded. Without that distinction, two different messages of different lengths can end up with the same padded form, and a forged message can be built from the code of an earlier one.
sections.plainLanguage: The basic version of this check takes the message, pads it out to a whole number of blocks, and encrypts each block one after another, feeding each result into the next. That works only when the message is always the same length, because the padding hides the difference between a message that filled the last block and one that did not.

sections.title: The AES-XCBC-MAC-96 Algorithm
sections.content:
The AES-XCBC-MAC-96 algorithm is a variant of the basic CBC-MAC with obligatory 10* padding, but it is secure for messages of arbitrary length. The calculations require numerous encryption operations, and this encryption must be accomplished using AES with a 128-bit key. Given a 128-bit secret key K, the algorithm is calculated for a message M that consists of n blocks M[1] to M[n], where the blocksize of the blocks M[1] to M[n-1] is 128 bits and the blocksize of the last block M[n] is between 1 and 128 bits.

The steps are as follows.

First, three 128-bit keys, K1, K2 and K3, are derived from the 128-bit secret key K, each by encrypting a fixed constant with K: 0x01010101010101010101010101010101 for K1, 0x02020202020202020202020202020202 for K2, and 0x03030303030303030303030303030303 for K3. The earlier published definition of K1 in the CBC-MAC paper uses a second encryption operation, but that is only needed for keys greater than 128 bits, so it is not part of this algorithm.

Second, E[0] is defined as 0x00000000000000000000000000000000. Third, for each block M[i] with i from 1 to n-1, the block is XORed with E[i-1] and the result is encrypted with K1, yielding E[i]. Fourth, the last block is treated according to its size. If it is a full 128 bits, it is XORed with E[n-1] and with K2, and the result is encrypted with K1, yielding E[n]. If it is shorter than 128 bits, it is first padded with a single 1 bit followed by the number of 0 bits, possibly none, needed to bring it to 128 bits, and then XORed with E[n-1] and with K3, and the result is encrypted with K1, yielding E[n].

The authenticator value is the leftmost 96 bits of the 128-bit E[n]. The K2 and K3 keys are what distinguish the two cases, and they are the reason the algorithm uses three keys: so that the length of the input stream does not need to be known in advance. If the message is the empty string, the message is padded and encrypted as in the short last block case to create M[1] and E[1]; this will never happen for ESP or AH, but is included for completeness.

Verification is performed by computing the entire 128-bit value on receipt and comparing the first 96 bits to the value stored in the authenticator field.

On padding, AES-XCBC-MAC-96 operates on 128-bit blocks of data, and the padding requirements of the CBC-MAC paper are part of the XCBC algorithm, so an implementation that follows that paper needs no additional padding. With regard to the implicit packet padding defined in the Authentication Header, no implicit packet padding is required.

On truncation, AES-XCBC-MAC produces a 128-bit authenticator value, and AES-XCBC-MAC-96 is derived by truncating that value as described for HMAC. For use with either ESP or AH, a truncated value using the first 96 bits must be supported, and no other authenticator value lengths are supported. The length of 96 bits was selected because it is the default authenticator length specified in the Authentication Header, and it meets the security requirements of the XCBC-MAC work.

On performance, for any CBC MAC variant the major computational effort is expended in computing the underlying block cipher. This algorithm uses a minimum number of AES invocations, one for each block of the message or fraction of one, giving performance equivalent to classic CBC-MAC. The key expansion requires three additional AES encryption operations, but these can be performed once in advance for each secret key.
sections.plainLanguage: The algorithm uses three keys derived from the secret key. Each block of the message is encrypted and chained into the next, exactly as before. What changes is the last block: if it is a full block, one derived key is mixed in, and if it is short, the message is padded and a different derived key is mixed in. The receiver can therefore tell the two cases apart, which is what stops one message being forged from another.

sections.title: Keying Material
sections.content:
AES-XCBC-MAC-96 is a secret key algorithm. For use with either ESP or AH a fixed key length of 128 bits must be supported, and key lengths other than 128 bits must not be supported, so only 128-bit keys are used.

The algorithm actually requires 384 bits of keying material, which is 128 bits for the AES key size plus twice the block size. That material can either be provided through the key generation mechanism or generated from a single 128-bit key. The latter approach has been selected, since it is analogous to other authenticators used within IPsec. The reason the algorithm uses three keys is so the length of the input stream does not need to be known in advance, which may be useful for systems that assemble large packets in one pass.

A strong pseudo-random function must be used to generate the required 128-bit key. That key, along with the three derived keys, should be used for no purposes other than those specified in the algorithm, and in particular they should not be used as keys in another cryptographic setting, because such abuses will invalidate the security of the authentication algorithm.

At the time of writing there are no specified weak keys for use with AES-XCBC-MAC-96, which does not mean to imply that weak keys do not exist. If a set of weak keys is identified, the use of those keys must be rejected, followed by a request for replacement keys or a newly negotiated security association.

The security architecture document describes the general mechanism for obtaining keying material when multiple keys are required for a single security association, for instance when an ESP security association requires a key for confidentiality and a key for authentication. In order to provide data origin authentication, the key distribution mechanism must ensure that unique keys are allocated and that they are distributed only to the parties taking part in the communication.

Current attacks do not necessitate a specific recommended frequency for key changes, but periodic key refreshment is a fundamental security practice: it helps against potential weaknesses of the function and the keys, reduces the information available to a cryptanalyst, and limits the damage resulting from a compromised key.
sections.plainLanguage: One 128-bit secret key is all a user has to manage. From it the algorithm derives the three keys it needs, and it tells implementers not to reuse them anywhere else, because doing so would weaken the authentication. The memo also says to change keys regularly, so that a stolen key does not do lasting damage.

sections.title: Test Vectors
sections.content:
The memo supplies seven test cases, provided by John Black, co-author of the XCBC-MAC algorithm, who verified them with two independent implementations. All values are hexadecimal. The cases cover an empty message, a message of 3 bytes, one of 16 bytes, one of 20 bytes, one of 32 bytes, one of 34 bytes, and one of 1000 bytes, so that both the exact-block case and the short-final-block case are exercised, including a message longer than a single block that ends part way through a block.

Each case gives the key, the message, the full 128-bit AES-XCBC-MAC value and the truncated 96-bit AES-XCBC-MAC-96 value. The key is the same in every case, 000102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f, which is also the message in the 16-byte case.
sections.plainLanguage: Seven worked examples let an implementer check their code against a known answer. They cover an empty message, a short one, exact multiples of the block size, and messages that end part way through a block.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security provided by AES-XCBC-MAC-96 is based on the strength of AES, and at the time of writing there are no practical cryptographic attacks against AES or against AES-XCBC-MAC-96.

As is true with any cryptographic algorithm, part of its strength lies in the correctness of the algorithm implementation, the security of the key management mechanism and its implementation, the strength of the associated secret key, and the correctness of the implementation in all of the participating systems. The document contains test vectors to assist in verifying the correctness of AES-XCBC-MAC-96 code.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo finds no practical attack against AES or against this construction. As with any cipher, though, much of the security depends on the code being written correctly and the key being kept secret, which is why the test vectors are given.

data.title: AES-XCBC-MAC-96
data.code:
(1)  Derive 3 128-bit keys (K1, K2 and K3) from the 128-bit secret
     key K, as follows:
     K1 = 0x01010101010101010101010101010101 encrypted with Key K
     K2 = 0x02020202020202020202020202020202 encrypted with Key K
     K3 = 0x03030303030303030303030303030303 encrypted with Key K

(2)  Define E[0] = 0x00000000000000000000000000000000

(3)  For each block M[i], where i = 1 ... n-1:
     XOR M[i] with E[i-1], then encrypt the result with Key K1,
     yielding E[i].

(4)  For block M[n]:

    a)  If the blocksize of M[n] is 128 bits:
        XOR M[n] with E[n-1] and Key K2, then encrypt the result with
        Key K1, yielding E[n].

    b)  If the blocksize of M[n] is less than 128 bits:

       i)  Pad M[n] with a single "1" bit, followed by the number of
           "0" bits (possibly none) required to increase M[n]'s
           blocksize to 128 bits.

       ii) XOR M[n] with E[n-1] and Key K3, then encrypt the result
           with Key K1, yielding E[n].

(5)  The authenticator value is the leftmost 96 bits of the 128-bit
     E[n].

items.title: Key length
items.text: 128 bits. Other key lengths must not be supported.

items.title: Keying material
items.text: 384 bits in total: the 128-bit AES key plus twice the block size.

items.title: Three derived keys
items.text: K1, K2 and K3, each the encryption of a fixed constant under the secret key.

items.title: Why three keys
items.text: So the length of the input stream does not have to be known in advance.

items.title: No reuse
items.text: The key and the three derived keys must not be used in any other cryptographic setting.

items.title: Refresh regularly
items.text: Periodic key refreshment limits the damage from a compromised key.
